ety.text: Borrowed from Latin ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ē- (“out of”) (short form of ex) + volvō (“roll”).

senses.d: To move (something) in regular procession through a system.
ex: The animal soul sooner expands and evolves it self to its full orb and extent than the humane Soul

senses.d: To change or transform (something).
ex: Over several years the author evolved the story originally drafted as a novella into a real epic.

senses.d: To cause (something) to come into being or develop.
ex: You will remove the pig, place it in the car, and drive it to my house in Wiltshire. That is the plan I have evolved.
[…]I ask you, rather, to evolve a suitable plan with due deliberation and report it to me."¹⁴

senses.d: To acquire or develop (a trait) in the process of biological evolution.
ex: How long ago did birds evolve beaks?

senses.d: To change genetic composition over successive generations through the process of evolution.
ex: A hundred thousand years from now, will Homo sapiens have evolved into beings unrecognizable to their ancestors?
The ice age was nearly two million years old by the time the woolly mammoth evolved.

senses.d: To give off (a gas such as carbon dioxide or oxygen) during a chemical reaction.
To wind or unwind (something).
To move in regular procession through a system.
ex: [T]he principles which Art involves, Science alone evolves.
Not by any power evolved from man's own resources, but by a power which descended from above.

senses.d: To change, to transform.
ex: What began as a few lines of code has now evolved into a million-line behemoth.
An aide of Shah told Reuters that Shah had an early penchant for poetry that evolved into an affinity for rap music.

senses.d: Of a trait; to develop within a population through biological evolution.
ex: How long ago did beaks evolve?

grp.label: move in regular procession through a system

fr:évoluer.gl: to evolve; to change, to develop

ety.text: Back-formation from évolution. Cf. also Latin ēvolvō.
From progrès + -er.
From progreso, from Latin prōgredior (“to proceed”). Cognate with Portuguese progredir.
From evolución + -ar.

chain.g: to evolve; to change, to develop
to roll forth or out; unroll, unfold

ety.text: Borrowed from French évoluer, from Latin ēvolvere. Doublet of evolver.
Borrowed from Latin prōgredior (“to proceed”), from prō + gradior (“step, walk”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese crecer, from Latin crēscere (“to grow”), from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”).

fr:élaborer.gl: to draw up, write up, make up, whip up, put together

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin ēlabōrāre. Cognate with Italian elaborare, Spanish elaborar.
From des- + arrollar, from Latin dis- (“not”) + rotulus (“roll of paper”).

Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old Galician-Portuguese des- Portuguese des- Portuguese envolver Portuguese desenvolver From des- + envolver.
Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin labōrō Latin ēlabōrārelbor. Portuguese elaborar Learned borrowing from Latin ēlabōrāre.

chain.g: the act of unrolling, unfolding or opening (of a book)

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiō, ēvolūtiōnis (“the act of unrolling, unfolding or opening (of a book)”), from ēvolūtus, perfect passive participle of ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ex + volvō (“roll”). Compare typologically Czech vývoj, Serbo-Croatian развој, Russian разви́ть (razvítʹ), развива́ть (razvivátʹ), разви́ться (razvítʹsja), развива́ться (razvivátʹsja), Russian разви́тие (razvítije), related to Proto-Slavic *viti (whence Czech vít, Russian вить (vitʹ)).

senses.d: A manoeuvre of troops or ships.
A turning movement, especially of the body.
ex: "Look now, that pirouette -- my stars! how Beauchamp would stare to see his darling perform such an evolution!"

senses.d: A turned or twisted shape; an involution, a complex or intricate shape.
The act or process of unfolding or opening out; the progression of events in regular succession.
The opening out of a curve; now more generally, the gradual transformation of a curve by a change of the conditions generating it.
The extraction of a root from a given power.
The act or an instance of giving off gas; emission.
ex: Allantoxaidin is decomposed on heating, with evolution of ammonia and cyanic acid.

senses.d: Development; the act or result of developing what was implicit in an idea, argument etc.
ex: The ongoing evolution of Lolita subculture fashion includes, among other things, the ballet style.
Suffering has a noble purpose: the evolution of consciousness and the burning up of the ego.

senses.d: A process of gradual change in a given system, subject, product etc., especially from simpler to more complex forms.
The transformation of animals, plants and other living things into different forms (now understood as a change in genetic composition) by the accumulation of changes over successive generations.

grp.label: general: a gradual process of development
military: One of a series of ordered movements
biology: change in the genetic composition of a population over time

chain.g: The act of unrolling or opening a book; reading.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiōnem (“unrolling, opening (a scroll)”, noun), derived from ēvolvō (“to unroll, unfold”).
Borrowed from French évolution, Latin ēvolūtiōnem (“unrolling of a book”), from ēvolvō (“to unfold, unroll, clear up”). Cognate with Catalan evolució.

chain.g: The act of unrolling or opening a book; reading.

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin ēvolūtiōnem. The expected form if derived by suffixation of evoluir + -ção would be *evoluição.
Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusder. Middle English -arie English -ary English evolutionary From evolution + -ary.

senses.d: Of or relating to the biological theory of evolution.
ex: The evolutionary history of marine mammals includes land-dwelling ancestors.

senses.d: Having formal similarities to the biological theory of evolution.
ex: The basic elements of an evolutionary growth theory are discussed in Section II.

ety.text: From évolution + -if.
From évolution + -aire.

chain.g: to roll forth or out; unroll, unfold

ety.text: Derived from Latin ēvolūtus (perfect passive participle of ēvolvō) + -ivo.
